From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
1976 novel by Jean Raspail
_**Le Jeu du Roi**_ ("the king's game") is a 1976 novel by the French writer [Jean Raspail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Raspail "Jean Raspail"). It focuses on the subject of the [Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Araucan%C3%ADa_and_Patagonia "Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia"). It was published by [éditions Robert Laffont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Robert_Laffont "Éditions Robert Laffont").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Jeu_du_Roi#cite_note-1)

# Le Jeu du Roi
## Adaptation
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Le_Jeu_du_Roi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Adaptation")]
The novel was the basis for the 1988 film _Letter from Patagonia_. The film was directed by [Marc Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Evans "Marc Evans") and stars [Pierre Dux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Dux "Pierre Dux").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Jeu_du_Roi#cite_note-2)

# _Blue Island_ (novel)
_**Blue Island**_ ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _**L'Île bleue**_) is a 1988 novel by the French writer [Jean Raspail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Raspail "Jean Raspail"). The narrative is set in [Touraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touraine "Touraine") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), where a charismatic boy gathers his friends on an island, where they play war games which become increasingly more interlinked with reality. The book was published in English in 1991, translated by Jeremy Leggatt.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Island_(novel)#cite_note-1)
The book was adapted into the 2001 television film _L'Île bleue_. The film was directed by [Nadine Trintignant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadine_Trintignant "Nadine Trintignant").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Island_(novel)#cite_note-2)

# _Blue Island_ (novel)
## Reception
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Blue_Island_(novel)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Reception")]
_[Kirkus Reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkus\_Reviews "Kirkus Reviews")_ described the books as "a touching story about coming of age under less-than-ideal circumstances. ... [T]he dovetailing here of adolescent bravado and cynicism with historical drama makes for a mostly satisfying mixture."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Island_(novel)#cite_note-3)_[Publishers Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers\_Weekly "Publishers Weekly")_ called it a "spellbinding fable", and wrote that "this is no myth-like _[Lord of the Flies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord\_of\_the\_Flies "Lord of the Flies")_. Contemporary history is an ever-present element, as German troops advance, France falls apart, the government evacuates Paris and refugees flood the countryside. ... Raspail (_[Who Will Remember the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Who\_Will\_Remember\_the\_People... "Who Will Remember the People...")_) narrowly avoids sentimentality in this powerful depiction of an end to innocence and illusion."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Island_(novel)#cite_note-4)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
1976 novel by Jean Raspail
_**Le Jeu du Roi**_ ("the king's game") is a 1976 novel by the French writer [Jean Raspail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Raspail "Jean Raspail"). It focuses on the subject of the [Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Araucan%C3%ADa_and_Patagonia "Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia"). It was published by [éditions Robert Laffont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89ditions_Robert_Laffont "Éditions Robert Laffont").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Jeu_du_Roi#cite_note-1)

## Adaptation
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Le_Jeu_du_Roi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Adaptation")]
The novel was the basis for the 1988 film _Letter from Patagonia_. The film was directed by [Marc Evans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Evans "Marc Evans") and stars [Pierre Dux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Dux "Pierre Dux").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Jeu_du_Roi#cite_note-2)

# Jean Raspail, right wing prophet of ‘identity politics’ has died
Jean Raspail | Fabrice Bluszez - Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
Published:June 30, 2020, 8:16 am
[Share](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/jean-raspail-right-wing-prophet-of-identity-politics-has-died/#/share)
Jean Raspail is author of the 1973 ‘Le Camp des Saints’ (The Camp of the Saints), a dystopian novel describing an invasion of immigrants from the Indian Subcontinent who land on the shores of Southern France in a flotilla of boats, then take control of the entire country. Raspail died on 12 June 2020, shortly before turning 95.
First translated into English in 1975, and still available in the 1994 edition by Social Contract Press, the novel has been quoted as a source of inspiration by Steve Bannon, [Stephen Miller](https://www.npr.org/2019/11/19/780552636/stephen-miller-and-the-camp-of-the-saints-a-white-nationalist-reference?ref=opendemocracy.net) and Rep. Steve King and has, so far, been re-published eight times in France, for the last time in 2011 with a foreword by the author, entitled ‘Big Other’.
It has often been compared to William Pierce’s ‘Turner Diaries’, although it lacks its rabid Antisemitism and does not reach the same climax of hysterical violence, even though it is also a book about the native French taking up arms against the ‘invaders’.

## Émile Zola
Lived Lived 1840 to 1902
From From French
Born in Born in Paris, France
Born Émile Édouard Charles Antoine Zola on April 2, 1840, in Paris to a Venetian-born engineer who designed the Zola Dam at Aix-en-Provence and a French mother, he lost his father at seven and was raised on a meagre pension in Provence, where he formed a lifelong friendship with the young Paul Cézanne. Returning to Paris, he failed his baccalauréat twice, worked as a clerk in a shipping firm, and joined the publisher Hachette, where he wrote literary and political journalism that did not hide his contempt for Napoleon III. Hachette dismissed him after the sordid autobiographical novel La Confession de Claude (1865) drew police attention. Thérèse Raquin (1867), a grim study of adultery and remorse, announced naturalism in the French novel. From 1871 he gave himself to Les Rougon-Macquart, a twenty-volume natural and social history of a family under the Second Empire, traced from peasant Plassans into mine, market, brothel, and battlefield. L'Assommoir (1877) made him wealthy. Nana (1880), Germinal (1885), and La Bête humaine (1890) followed. He wrote every day for thirty years under the motto nulla dies sine linea, no day without a line. On January 13, 1898, he published J'accuse on the front page of L'Aurore, his open letter to the President of the Republic exposing the army's frame-up of the Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus. He was convicted of libel and fled to a year in England. He died at home in Paris on the night of September 28, 1902, asphyxiated by a blocked chimney, aged sixty-two. The roofer responsible, decades later, confessed to a friend that he had done it for the army.

## Émile Zola
Lived Lived 1840 to 1902
From From French
Born in Born in Paris, France
Born Émile Édouard Charles Antoine Zola on April 2, 1840, in Paris to a Venetian-born engineer who designed the Zola Dam at Aix-en-Provence and a French mother, he lost his father at seven and was raised on a meagre pension in Provence, where he formed a lifelong friendship with the young Paul Cézanne. Returning to Paris, he failed his baccalauréat twice, worked as a clerk in a shipping firm, and joined the publisher Hachette, where he wrote literary and political journalism that did not hide his contempt for Napoleon III. Hachette dismissed him after the sordid autobiographical novel La Confession de Claude (1865) drew police attention. Thérèse Raquin (1867), a grim study of adultery and remorse, announced naturalism in the French novel. From 1871 he gave himself to Les Rougon-Macquart, a twenty-volume natural and social history of a family under the Second Empire, traced from peasant Plassans into mine, market, brothel, and battlefield. L'Assommoir (1877) made him wealthy. Nana (1880), Germinal (1885), and La Bête humaine (1890) followed. He wrote every day for thirty years under the motto nulla dies sine linea, no day without a line. On January 13, 1898, he published J'accuse on the front page of L'Aurore, his open letter to the President of the Republic exposing the army's frame-up of the Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus. He was convicted of libel and fled to a year in England. He died at home in Paris on the night of September 28, 1902, asphyxiated by a blocked chimney, aged sixty-two. The roofer responsible, decades later, confessed to a friend that he had done it for the army.
